paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMGZ-00 — Introduction: 'War without Gun Smoke': China's Paranaval Challenge in the Maritime Gray Zone (Erickson & Martinson, 2019)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Authored by CMSI Research Director Dr. Andrew S. Erickson and CMSI researcher Ryan D. Martinson as the introduction to *China's Maritime Gray Zone Operations* (Naval Institute Press, 2019, Ebook pp. 19–31), `CMGZ-00` synthesizes the May 2–3, 2017 CMSI conference at the U.S. Naval War College. The authors argue that Beijing conducts 'maritime rights protection' (`海上维权`) in the Yellow, East, and South China Seas through a coordinated three-force architecture—deploying the world's largest coast guard ('white-hulled' **CCG**) and maritime militia ('blue-hulled' **PAFMM**) on the front lines to alter the status quo via nonlethal coercion ('a war without gun smoke' / `一场没有硝烟的战争`), while keeping the world's largest navy by hull count ('gray-hulled' **PLAN**) over the horizon to deter adversary escalation.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Conceptualizing the Gray Zone (pp. 1–2)**: Synthesizes Part I's theoretical, strategic, doctrinal, and legal chapters: Michael Petersen's distinction between Phases 0–I gray-zone operations and Phases II–V hybrid warfare; Peter Dutton's 'two restraints and two asymmetries'; Dale Rielage and Austin Strange's finding that 'people's war at sea' (`海上人民战争`) is treated by Chinese strategists as a high-end wartime doctrine rather than a guide for peacetime rights protection, which instead follows the **'PLA–law enforcement–militia joint defense system' (`军警民联防机制`)** balancing *weiquan* and *weiwen*; and Jonathan Odom's international-law proof that PAFMM actions are legally attributable to the PRC and violate COLREGs and UNCLOS.
• **China's Coast Guard & Maritime Militia (pp. 2–4)**: Tracks the CCG's evolution from the 2013 four-agency merger to its **July 2018 incorporation into the People's Armed Police (PAP)** and its fleet of **>225 offshore ships (>500 tons)**—exceeding Japan (~80), the USCG (~50), and South Korea (~45) combined, led by two **>10,000-ton *Zhaotou*-class** cutters and projected to hit **260 ships by 2020**. Details the post-2015 professionalization of the PAFMM, including **Sansha City's 84 purpose-built vessels** with water cannons and external ramming rails, peacetime/wartime ISR roles (Mark Stokes), and wartime limitations (Clemens & Weber).
• **Near-Seas Scenarios & Policy Options (pp. 4–5)**: Reviews South and East China Sea scenarios (Glaser & Funaiole; Liff; Yamamoto), highlights the **August 2018 DoD China Military Power Report** validating CMSI's PAFMM research and confirming PAFMM involvement in the 2016 Senkaku surge, and contrasts Vietnam's risky operational resistance during the **2014 HYSY-981 oil rig incident** (Moreland) with U.S. policy options for empowering front-line nonlethal responses alongside allies.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Indigenous Chinese Gray-Zone Concepts**: 'Safeguarding maritime rights and interests' (`维护海洋权益` / `海上维权`); 'Low-intensity maritime rights protection struggle' (`低强度海上维权斗争`, *National Defense* Jan 2017); 'War without gun smoke' (`一场没有硝烟的战争`); 'PLA–law enforcement–militia joint defense system' (`军警民联防机制`: 1st line militia `一线民兵`, 2nd line MLE `二线行政执法`, 3rd line PLA `三线部队`); Seaborne Maritime Militia (`海上民兵`) vs. Coastal Defense Militia (`海防民兵`) and PLA Army Coastal Defense Brigades (`海防旅`, *PLA Military Terms* 2011, p. 334).
• **Force-Structure Benchmarks**: **CCG Offshore Fleet (>500t)**: `>225` hulls in 2018 (`260` projected by 2020) vs. Japan `~80`, USCG `~50`, South Korea `~45`; `2` *Zhaotou*-class cutters (`>10,000 tons` full load); **Sansha City PAFMM**: `84` purpose-built vessels with water cannons and ramming rails.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
All 4 reference rows (`CMGZ00-R01` to `CMGZ00-R04`) are rated `ok` (noting two Chinese character typesetting splits in Notes 2 and 4 on p. 6: `'军事禾斗学出版华土'` for `军事科学出版社` and `'氐强度'` for `低强度`). Together with `CMGZ-P1` (Doc #52), `CMGZ-00` provides the conceptual foundation for the 2026 China Coast Guard and survey-vessel operations east of Taiwan documented in Batch 2's **CMSI-N21** and Batch 5's **CIPI-DS26**.

**Footnote rows**: all 7 footnotes were extracted and added to the Reference Audit Matrix as source rows (CMGZ00-N001 to CMGZ00-N007), each with its citing sentence and the result of the check. Footnote-level result: 7 notes: 3 (43%) are confirmed, 1 of them against a retrieved source and 2 after an outside web search (1 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 4 (57%) are not confirmed. Of the 4 notes not confirmed, 2 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 2 were judged not web-checkable (2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation). A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 7 source rows are 3 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 4 `unk`. 3 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CMGZ-P1 — Part I: Conceptualizing the Gray Zone (Petersen; Dutton; Rielage & Strange; Odom, 2019)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part I (Chapters 1–4, Ebook pp. 32–96, 35 PDF pages, 165 endnotes) of *China's Maritime Gray Zone Operations* (ed. Andrew S. Erickson and Ryan D. Martinson, Naval Institute Press, 2019), `CMGZ-P1` brings together Michael B. Petersen, Peter A. Dutton, Dale C. Rielage & Austin M. Strange, and Jonathan G. Odom to establish a rigorous four-part foundation—theoretical, strategic, Chinese-doctrinal, and international-legal—for understanding China's paranaval coercion in the East and South China Seas.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 1 — The Chinese Maritime Gray Zone (Michael B. Petersen, PDF pp. 2–10, 33 notes)**: Uses the March 2009 *USNS Impeccable* incident to illustrate Mazarr's three gray-zone characteristics (revisionism, ambiguity, gradualism / Schelling's 'salami tactics'), highlights civilianization of contested features, distinguishes **Phases 0–I gray-zone activities** (where the PLAN acts as an over-the-horizon deterrent) from **Phases II–V hybrid/compound war** (where military force compels, as in Ukraine) in **Exhibit 1-1**, and exposes the **inverted escalation dynamic** whereby less-lethal PAFMM trawlers act more aggressively than warships.
• **Ch. 2 — Conceptualizing China's Maritime Gray Zone Operations (Peter A. Dutton, PDF pp. 11–14, 12 notes)**: Defines China's three maritime aims (security buffer rings, marine resources, regional rule-making), reconstructs the **April 2012 Scarborough Reef model**, and formulates **'two restraints and two asymmetries'**: U.S. stability-focused restraint + Chinese time-for-space patience, paired with China's regional paranaval overmatch + the U.S. lack of forward-deployed coast guard or militia forces at the lower rungs of the escalation ladder.
• **Ch. 3 — Is the Maritime Militia Prosecuting a People's War at Sea? (Dale C. Rielage & Austin M. Strange, PDF pp. 15–22, 38 notes)**: Traces the Maoist history of the maritime militia (1950s–1978) and uses a **bibliometric audit (Exhibit 3-1)** to prove that while PAFMM literature exploded after 2013, `'people's war at sea'` (`海上人民战争`) appeared **zero times** in *People's Navy* from Jan 2010 to Sept 2017 and in only **53 CNKI articles**—confirming it is a marginal wartime concept, whereas peacetime gray-zone operations follow the **'three-line rights protection law enforcement formation' (`三线维权执法格局`)**.
• **Ch. 4 — When Gray Zone Meets Black Letter (Jonathan G. Odom, PDF pp. 23–35, 82 notes)**: Proves under the 2001 ILC *State Responsibility Articles* (Arts. 4, 5, 8) that CCG and PAFMM actions are legally attributable to the PRC; proves under the ICJ's **'critical date'** doctrine that post-crystallization gray-zone acts are **legally 'meaningless'** for strengthening territorial sovereignty claims; and details PRC breaches of **UNCLOS Arts. 56, 58, and 94** and **COLREGs Rules 2, 6, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16, and 18**.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
Of the 4 chapter-level reference rows audited in `CMGZ-P1`, 3 are rated `ok` and **1 is rated `fix` (`[CMGZP1-R01]`)**:
• **`[CMGZP1-R01]` (`fix` — Placing the Crimean Bridge Terminus in 'Krasnoyarsk' Instead of 'Krasnodar', PDF p. 4)**: On p. 4, Petersen writes that Russia's Kerch Strait 'Crimean Bridge' connects Crimea directly from `'its province of Krasnoyarsk'`—confusing **Krasnodar Krai (`Краснодарский край`)** on the Black/Azov Sea with **Krasnoyarsk Krai (`Красноярский край`)** in central Siberia ~4,000 km away!
• **Additional Slips Logged (`ok · slip`)**: Ch. 1 Note 19 dates a Jan 2017 *Diplomat* URL to `'January 21, 2016'`; Ch. 3 Notes 4/30/34 print `'军事禾斗学出版社'`, `'Jinghai City'` (for Qionghai City), and `'[Ge Hongyong]'` (for Ge Yonghong); and Ch. 4 Notes 4/64/82 print `'Mazaar'` and `'no. 411'` (for `'no. 3'`).

**Footnote rows**: all 167 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 132 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CMGZP1-S1N001 to CMGZP1-N081). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 167 notes: 81 (49%) are confirmed, 10 of them against a retrieved source and 71 after an outside web search (56 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 2 are flagged for reader check; 86 (51%) are not confirmed. Of the 86 notes not confirmed, 14 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 4 were judged not web-checkable (1 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 1 print-only book or paywalled item; 2 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation); 68 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 132 source rows are 60 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 72 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CMGZP1-S2N028`: The sentence says seventy Vietnamese perished in the 1988 naval battle near Johnson South Reef. Most sources, including Vietnamese accounts, give 64 dead, some also list nine captured; one academic account gives 64 to 70 killed; `CMGZP1-S2N032`: The sentence says Lassen was subjected to "provocative" maneuvering by a small Chinese "commercial" craft and other vessels, almost assuredly crewed by maritime militia, that dangerously crossed its path. 38 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Ch. 1 (Mulvenon): PLA Fuel Conservation ('Love Oil as Blood', +10B RMB 2006 Fuel Overrun), First PLAN U.S. Mainland Visit Fuel-Line Failure (Oiler Nancang AO 953), 3-Stage SPR Plan (Zhenhai/Daishan/Huangdao/Dalian), Wartime POL Reserves (65% Gasoline), and Note 33's '200,000 Billion Barrels' Unit Error (PDF pp. 2–8, Ch. 1 Notes 1–33)
rows.usage: Examines PLA strategic/operational/tactical energy equities, the 10B RMB ($1.3B) 2006 fuel cost overrun (2006 Defense White Paper), oiler Nancang (AO 953) breaking a fuel line en route to the U.S. mainland (requiring PACOM helicopter delivery, Note 17), China's 4 coastal SPR bases aiming for 90 days by 2020, PLA war-preparation vs. normal-use reserves, and Note 33's statement that 3–6% annual oil demand growth adds 'more than 200,000 billion barrels to demand each year'.
rows.finding: Substantive unit error in Endnote 33 (`fix`): While Mulvenon's PLA POL mobilization, SPR, and *Nancang* logistics insights are exceptional, **Endnote 33 (PDF p. 8) states that 3–6% annual oil demand growth adds `'more than 200,000 billion barrels to demand each year'`**—a million-fold unit error for **~200,000 barrels per day (bpd)** (or ~73–200 million barrels/year; total global proven oil reserves in 2006 were ~1,200 billion barrels). Also notes the Chinese homophone typo `'战备油料处被'` for `'战备油料储备'` on p. 6.

rows.source: Ch. 2 (Freeman) & Ch. 3 (Rosen & Houser): U.S. vs. China Oil Import Vulnerability (12M bpd / 70% / 27% World Trade vs. 3.8M bpd / <50% / <6% World Trade; >65% Coal) and China's 2005–2006 Macroeconomic Baseline ($2.7T GDP, 49.8% Industry, 42.6–50%+ Investment, 21% Bank-Financed FAI, $177B Surplus) (PDF pp. 9–23, Ch. 2 Note 1 & Ch. 3 Notes 1–9)
rows.usage: Freeman contrasts U.S. oil import dependence (12M bpd, ~70% of consumption, 27% of world trade, Katrina knocking out 10% of U.S. refining) with China's coal-dominated energy diet (>65% coal, 3.8M bpd oil imports) and 7–11.5x worse energy efficiency than Japan (4.5x worse than U.S.); Rosen & Houser audit China's 2006 GDP ($2.7T = 5% of $44.4T world GDP), sectoral split (49.8% industry, 39.2% services, 11% agriculture), expenditure split (42.6% FAI in 2005, >50% in 2006 with only 21% bank-financed; 38% consumption; $177B net export surplus), and 40%/60% urban/rural demographics.
rows.finding: Verified (`ok`): All EIU, BEA, CEIC, World Bank, and PIIE macroeconomic figures and sectoral shares (49.8 + 39.2 + 11.0 = 100.0%) check out.

rows.source: Ch. 4 (Pietz) & Ch. 5 (Herberg): IEA 2030 Energy Supply/Demand Tables (Tables 1–7: 139 Overseas NOC Deals, 10–15% Equity Oil, 102.5M bbl Phase 1 SPR) and China's LNG & Eurasian Pipeline Geopolitics (2% -> 8% Gas Share by 2020, Guangdong/Fujian Terminals, Sakhalin-2 & <2% Total Energy Vulnerability to LNG Embargo) (PDF pp. 24–52, Ch. 4 Notes 1–20 & Ch. 5 Notes 1–24)
rows.usage: Pietz compiles IEA World Energy Outlook 2004/2006 projections (Tables 1–5), Lieberthal & Herberg's tally of 139 overseas NOC deals across 7 regions (Table 6: 37 Africa, 31 SE Asia, 25 Middle East, 21 Eurasia, 16 Latin America, 6 North America, 3 NE Asia = 139 total, 100%), CNOOC Ltd.'s 70.64%/29.36% ownership split, and Phase 1 SPR capacities (Table 7: Zhenhai 33M + Aoshan 31.5M + Huangdao 19M + Dalian 19M = 102.5M bbl); Herberg analyzes China's LNG terminals (Guangdong 6 mmt/y, Fujian 3 mmt/y), Gazprom's Sakhalin-2 takeover, and why a naval LNG embargo would affect at most 20% of China's gas (<2% of total energy).
rows.finding: Verified with a minor endnote name typo (`ok · slip`): Table 6 deal counts (`21+25+37+3+31+16+6 = 139`) and percentages (`15+18+27+2+22+11+4 = 99/100%`) and Table 4 demand totals (`1354+636+636+73+63+236+20 = 3018 Mtoe`) sum accurately; Ch. 4 Note 1 misspells **Angus Maddison** as `'Agnus Maddison'`.

rows.source: Ch. 6 (Collins & Erickson): 'National Oil, Nationally Carried' Tanker Push (>40 VLCCs Needed vs. 18 In Service), Table 1 Oil Transport Costs ($1.14/bbl VLCC vs. $2.14 Pipeline vs. $7.19 Rail), 31 of 42 New VLCCs PRC-Flagged, Convoy (>25 Escorts for 14 VLCCs/wk) & Blockade/War-Risk Insurance Math ($8.9–$13.3M/day), and Page 55's '$270 Million' Maritime Trade Unit Error (PDF pp. 53–74, Ch. 6 Notes 1–86)
rows.usage: Evaluates China's VLCC fleet (18 VLCCs vs. 100 Japan, 47 ROK, 43 USA; 31 of 42 VLCCs on order slated for PRC flag; 29.6% of global tanker orderbook), Table 1 transport cost comparison ($1.14/bbl VLCC vs. $2.14 pipeline vs. $7.19 train), 35-day Persian Gulf convoy math (>25 surface escorts for 14 VLCCs/week), distant blockade barriers (52 tankers/day in Malacca, 30x at-sea cargo resales), War Risk insurance spikes (7.5–10% of $130M ship value/day = $8.9–$13.3M/day), and p. 55's statement that China's maritime trade could equal $1T by 2020, 'nearly four times the 2006 figure of $270 million (10 percent of China's gross domestic product)'.
rows.finding: Substantive unit error on page 55 (`fix`): While the tanker economics, convoy math and normal-rate insurance calculations are sound (Table 1's transport costs are a graphic in the uploaded PDF and could not be re-extracted), **page 55 states that China's 2006 maritime trade was `'$270 million (10 percent of China's gross domestic product)'`**—a thousand-fold unit error for **$270 billion** (10% of China's $2.7 trillion 2006 GDP and one-fourth of $1 trillion)! Second, smaller discrepancy found on re-check (p. 69): the chapter's war-risk figures do not follow from its own inputs — 7.5–10 percent of a $130 million VLCC's value per day is $9.75–$13.0 million, not the printed $8.9–$13.3 million (which are the normal-rate daily figures of $8,900–$13,300 multiplied by 1,000), so the $26.7–$39.9 million three-day totals carry the same discrepancy.

rows.source: China’s 1993 oil-import transition and 2003 world rankings
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “China became a net oil importer in 1993 and a decade later was the second-largest-consuming and third-largest-importing nation.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The contemporary Senate hearing places the overtaking of Japan in consumption in late 2003. The IEA 2003 monthly reports discuss adjustments for unreported refining and trade, which affect comparisons. The consumption rank and the 1993 net-import transition do not supply a matched worldwide 2003 import ranking. Crude-only and total-petroleum imports, and gross and net imports, cannot be substituted for one another.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A 2003 international import table with product scope and net/gross definition matching the chapter.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Contemporaneous U.S. government testimony confirms that China switched from net exporter in 1993 and overtook Japan as the second-largest petroleum consumer in 2003. Leverett’s 2006 testimony puts China third among oil importers at the time of his testimony. That later ranking cannot establish the 2003 import rank. The 2003 rank needs a same-year table with a consistent definition of net petroleum imports. Rechecked November 14, 2026. The IEA trade table for the fourth quarter of 2002 ranks Germany third. It is a useful close-in comparator and cannot establish the full-year 2003 rank. The timing of the importer transition and production-consumption comparison are separately sourced. Retain the 2003 ranking as open until a full-year same-definition table is found. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. Tie the rank to net petroleum imports and the calendar year. The IEA’s available contemporaneous ranked table is a quarterly comparator and the congressional source gives a later ranking. Comparing those figures confirms that the 2003 worldwide rank still requires the full annual table. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. Separate the two 2003 rankings. The State Department account describes China surpassing Japan in consumption. The 2006 hearing describes its import rank in a later period. A 2003 net-import table for all countries, using one petroleum definition, is still needed. Source recheck. Contemporary testimony in the 2005 Senate hearing explicitly places China’s overtaking Japan in oil consumption in late 2003. That provides a dated primary confirmation of the consumption rank. It does not report a comparable 2003 worldwide net-import ranking. The unresolved portion remains the import rank and whether it covers crude alone or all petroleum.

rows.source: China’s oil import dependence: baseline and projected range
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “If predictions hold true about the increase in China’s dependence on foreign oil from its current level of 40 percent to 60–80 percent in the next decade or so, then Beijing’s vulnerability will only get worse over time, not better.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The 2006 NEA-hosted analysis reports a 43% starting dependence and a 60% projection for 2020. The 2010 Commerce speech and later crude-import series use different dates and product definitions. They cannot authenticate the chapter’s full 60–80% forecast band. In particular, later observed crude dependence is not proof that an earlier forecast used the same oil basket, scenario or endpoint.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** An identifiable contemporary forecaster, oil definition and target year for the 80% upper endpoint.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** A 2010 Commerce Ministry speech reports 41% for 2005, and a 2006 analysis hosted by the energy administration reports 43% for the preceding year and projects 60% by 2020. These support an approximately 40% baseline and the lower end of the projected range. The 80% endpoint, its target year and the precise dependence measure remain unconfirmed. Rechecked November 14, 2026. A retrospective government release gives 73.6% for crude-oil import dependence in 2020, inside the projected band. That result supports the direction of change on the crude-oil measure. It cannot establish the exact scope and horizon of the original forecast, or independently verify the paper's vulnerability assessment. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. Compare the Commerce Ministry’s 41% baseline and the energy administration’s 43% figure with the later 73.6% crude measure only after identifying the denominator. The later observation is consistent with growth and the broad band. It does not establish when, by whom or for what series the upper endpoint was projected. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The two contemporaneous Chinese government sources put the starting estimate near 40%. Preserve the 60% projection as a separately attributable figure. The 80% upper bound still lacks a forecast issuer, scenario and endpoint. Later crude-dependent ratios use a narrower product category.

rows.source: The 2020 natural-gas share target and annual growth assumption
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “Current plans call for double-digit annual rates of growth in gas use and for gas to make up 8 percent of energy demand by 2020.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** A newly recovered April 2006 CSIS analysis discusses officials wanting an 8% gas share, but that passage does not independently establish the exact official 2020 instrument. The contemporary APEC outlook instead distinguishes a government aspiration of 10–15% in 2020 from its own modeled 6% in 2020 and 8% in 2030. These are distinct scenarios and dates, not interchangeable confirmations. Later domestic production growth also does not verify the chapter’s forecast of gas-use growth.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The actual pre-publication plan specifying 8% by 2020 and a defined demand-growth interval.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** A later State Council programme under the 13th Five-Year Plan targeted about 10% of total energy consumption from gas by 2020. The IEA records an 18% increase in Chinese gas demand in 2018, which is an observed annual result. Neither establishes what the earlier plan cited in the chapter called for. The 8% target and sustained double-digit growth assumption still need contemporaneous policy documentation. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The two note 1 references date to 2002 and May 2005. They are forecasts or analyses that predate the later 13th Plan. The 2015 target in CMS10-R08 and 2020 target here should not be harmonized on the basis of a common percentage. Locate the scenario table and energy-demand denominator. The recovered May 2005 LBNL paper recommends gas market development, but the retrieved material does not tie the chapter's 8% figure to a specified official target. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. A contemporary Chatham House study reproduces a revised Energy Research Institute projection of 9% in 2020 alongside earlier scenarios. That is evidence of competing contemporary targets. The cited 8% and annual growth assumption still need an exact scenario or controlling plan provision. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The plan and IEA series cited in the audit measure a 2020 target and an observed one-year growth rate under later policies. Look for the pre-publication plan or forecast behind the 8% target and its assumed growth interval. Each figure needs its own attribution. Source recheck. The contemporary Eleventh Plan targets a 2010 share, while a later official source documents 4.3% in the 2010 energy mix and average annual domestic production growth of 14% for 2005–10. Production growth is a different variable from the chapter’s projected growth in gas use. The pre-publication source for the 8% by 2020 target and its demand-growth interval remains to be identified.

rows.source: China’s tanker capacity serving foreign customers
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “At present an estimated 90 percent of China’s oil shipping capacity serves foreign clients.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The author’s 2007 Orbis article repeats the 90% foreign-customer estimate and points to the same contemporary debate. A second publication by the same author/source chain is not independent verification. Capacity serving foreign clients is not the inverse of China’s import cargo carried by foreign vessels; fleet size and charter allocation use different denominators.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A dated operator/charter allocation dataset stating fleet scope, capacity metric and customer classification.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** The contemporary Orbis article repeats the estimate about the share of Chinese oil-shipping capacity serving foreign customers. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CES-P1 — Part I: China's Energy Future and National Security Strategy (Mulvenon; Freeman; Rosen & Houser; Pietz; Herberg; Collins & Erickson, 2008/2012)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part I (Chapters 1–6, Ebook pp. 19–128, 74 PDF pages, 173 endnotes) of *China's Energy Strategy: The Impact on Beijing's Maritime Policies* (ed. Gabriel B. Collins, Andrew S. Erickson, Lyle J. Goldstein, and William S. Murray, Naval Institute Press, 2008 / 2012 Ebook ed.), `CES-P1` brings together eight specialists to subject China's 'Malacca Dilemma,' overseas equity oil acquisitions, LNG/pipeline plans, and state tanker fleet buildup to rigorous military, macroeconomic, and shipping-market scrutiny. Together, the six chapters prove that (1) domestic coal (~65–90% of primary energy) insulates China's overall economy far more than commonly assumed; (2) Chinese National Oil Companies (CNPC, Sinopec, CNOOC) and tanker operators (COSCO, China Merchants) act primarily as profit-maximizing commercial players in a global, fungible oil market; and (3) neither a PLAN convoy defense of Persian Gulf tankers nor a distant U.S. Navy oil blockade of China at the Strait of Malacca is operationally or economically viable short of total global war.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 1 — The PLA Perspective (James Mulvenon, PDF pp. 2–8, 33 notes)**: Examines PLA strategic inputs (11th Five-Year Plan), operational debates ('free-riding' on USN SLOC security vs. distrust after the 1993 *Yinhe* incident, while oiler *Nancang* AO 953 broke a fuel line on its first U.S. mainland visit), tactical fuel conservation (+10B RMB 2006 PLA fuel cost overrun), the 4-site coastal **Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR)** (Zhenhai, Daishan, Huangdao, Dalian, targeting 90 days / 40–50M tons by 2020), and PLA war-preparation vs. normal-use POL reserves (gasoline = 65% of wartime supplies).
• **Ch. 2 — Energy as China's Achilles' Heel? (Chas W. Freeman Jr., PDF pp. 9–13, 1 note)**: Contrasts U.S. oil import dependence (~12M bpd, ~70% of consumption, 27% of world trade) with China's (3.8M bpd, <50% of oil consumption, <6% of world trade, >65% coal), warning that U.S. SLOC interdiction would trigger global Lloyd's insurance shocks, retaliatory strikes on concentrated U.S. refineries, and supplier embargoes.
• **Ch. 3 — Scenarios for the Chinese Economy (Daniel H. Rosen & Trevor Houser, PDF pp. 14–23, 9 notes)**: Audits China's 2006 $2.7T economy (49.8% industry, 39.2% services, 11% agriculture; 42.6–50%+ investment share with only 21% bank-financed; $177B trade surplus; 40% urban / 60% rural) and comparative disadvantages (Table 1).
• **Ch. 4 — Past, Present & Future of China's Energy Sector (David Pietz, PDF pp. 24–40, 20 notes)**: Tracks IEA 2030 projections (Tables 1–5), China's 2002–2003 energy-intensity spike (consuming 40% of world cement, 25% of aluminum, 20% of steel at 3x world average energy intensity), the 1998 CNPC/Sinopec reorganization, **139 overseas NOC deals** (Table 6; equity oil = 10–15% of imports), CNOOC Ltd.'s post-Unocal shareholder vote, and Phase 1 SPR capacity (Table 7: 102.5M barrels).
• **Ch. 5 — Geopolitics of China's LNG Development (Mikkal Herberg, PDF pp. 41–52, 24 notes)**: Shows why gas (rising from 2% to 8% of China's energy by 2020, 40% imported via pipelines and Asia-Pacific LNG terminals at Guangdong and Fujian) poses far lower strategic vulnerability than oil: a naval embargo on seaborne LNG would affect at most ~20% of China's gas (<2% of total energy).
• **Ch. 6 — Chinese Efforts to Create a National Tanker Fleet (Gabriel B. Collins & Andrew S. Erickson, PDF pp. 53–74, 86 notes)**: Audits the `'national oil, nationally carried'` (`国油国运`) push (>40 VLCCs needed vs. 18 in service; 31 of 42 new VLCCs slated for PRC flag; 29.6% of global tanker orderbook), proves in **Table 1** that seaborne VLCC transport ($1.14/bbl) is far cheaper than pipelines ($2.14/bbl) or rail ($7.19/bbl), calculates that convoying 14 VLCCs/week from the Persian Gulf requires **>25 surface escorts** (beyond PLAN capability), and shows why 52 tankers/day in Malacca, 30x at-sea cargo resales, and **War Risk insurance spikes of roughly $9–$13M/day** (the chapter prints $8.9–$13.3M) make a distant blockade unworkable.

sections.body:
• **Energy & Macroeconomic Benchmarks**: 2006 China GDP: `$2.7 trillion` (`49.8%` industry, `39.2%` services, `11%` agriculture; `42.6–50%+` FAI [`21%` bank-financed]; `$177B` trade surplus); Energy intensity: `3x` world average (`4.7x` U.S., `11.5x` Japan; `40%` of world cement, `25%` aluminum, `20%` steel); 2006 PLA fuel cost overrun: `+10 billion RMB` (`~$1.3B`); Wartime gasoline share: `65%` of wartime supplies; Phase 1 SPR (Table 7): Zhenhai `33.0M bbl`, Aoshan `31.5M bbl`, Huangdao `19.0M bbl`, Dalian `19.0M bbl` = `102.5M bbl` (targeting `90 days` / `40–50M tons` by 2020); Overseas NOC deals (Table 6): `139` deals (`10–15%` equity oil share of imports).
• **Tanker, Convoy & Insurance Benchmarks (Ch. 6)**: **Sample Oil Transport Costs to China (Table 1)**: VLCC Ras Tanura–Ningbo (`7,000 km`) = `$1.14/bbl` (`$0.163/1,000 km`) vs. Pipeline Angarsk–Skovorodino (`2,700 km`) = `$2.14/bbl` (`$0.793/1,000 km`) vs. Train Angarsk–Manzhouli (`1,000 km`) = `$7.19/bbl`; **VLCC Fleets (Fig. 3)**: Japan `100`, South Korea `47`, U.S. `43`, Germany `20`, China `18` (`31 of 42` new Chinese VLCCs on order slated to fly PRC flag); **Convoy Math**: `14` VLCCs/week on a `35-day` Persian Gulf cycle requires `>25` surface warships; **Malacca Traffic**: `52` oil tankers/day; **VLCC Hull Insurance ($130M ship)**: normal `2.5–3.75%/yr` (`$8,900–$13,300/day`) vs. War Risk Exclusion Zone `7.5–10%/day` (`$8.9–$13.3 million/day` as printed, or `$26.7–$39.9 million` for 3 days in the Persian Gulf; 7.5–10% of $130M actually works out to $9.75–$13.0 million/day).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
The initial four claim audits identified two significant unit corrections:
• **`[CESP1-R01]` (`fix` — 'More Than 200,000 Billion Barrels to Demand Each Year' Unit Error in Ch. 1 Note 33, PDF p. 8)**: Mulvenon writes that 3–6% annual oil demand growth adds `'more than 200,000 billion barrels to demand each year'`—a million-fold unit error for **~200,000 barrels per day (bpd)**.
• **`[CESP1-R04]` (`fix` — '$270 Million' for '$270 Billion' as 10% of China's 2006 GDP in Ch. 6, PDF p. 55)**: Collins and Erickson write that China's 2006 maritime trade was `'$270 million (10 percent of China's gross domestic product)'`—a thousand-fold unit error for **$270 billion**.
• **Secondary observation on `[CESP1-R04]`**: The chapter's War Risk insurance range ($8.9–$13.3 million/day) does not equal 7.5–10% of the $130 million ship value it cites ($9.75–$13.0 million/day); the printed range is the normal-rate daily range multiplied by 1,000.

**Oil production and industry history**: In the recovered CIA World Factbook ranking, China produced 3.631 million barrels per day in 2005, or 3.63 million rounded, and ranked sixth. Cite that edition when reporting the rank (CESP1-R55). Sinopec’s 2002 Form 20-F describes the state-created 1983 predecessor as having primary responsibility for refining and petrochemicals. Its precise national refining share in 1983 remains unverified (CESP1-R43). Separate the documented 1998 asset reorganization and later issuer-specific offerings from the characterization of the 1999 sector-wide plan as a debt-for-equity swap. That characterization still needs the policy instrument or the relevant debt-conversion schedules (CESP1-R45, CESP1-R46).

**Footnote rows**: all 177 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 138 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CESP1-S1N001 to CESP1-N086). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 177 notes: 37 (21%) are confirmed, 0 of them against a retrieved source and 37 after an outside web search (30 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 17 are flagged for reader check; 140 (79%) are not confirmed. Of the 140 notes not confirmed, 28 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 16 were judged not web-checkable (6 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 3 private interviews or conversations; 6 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 1 other item); 96 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 138 source rows are 26 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 112 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CESP1-S1N024`: The sentence says a March 2001 report stated China would invest 20 billion RMB during the 10th Five-Year Plan to establish a strategic reserve by 2003. Sources confirm the 2001 plan and 2003 target but one 2007 report puts investment in the first four bases at about 6 billion yuan; the ChinaOnline report of 30 March 2001 was…; `CESP1-S1N027`: The sentence cites APERC for targets of 35 days of imports (14 days government, 21 days state enterprises) and 50 days by 2010. Retrieved sources give a 25-day initial plan (2003), 55 days by 2015 and 90 days by 2020 (OGJ 2005), and a three-phase target of 90 days of net imports (ORF); these may come from different plan vintages; `CESP1-S1N033`: The sentence says China's dependence on foreign oil would rise from its current level of 40 percent to 60 to 80 percent in the next decade or so. The Ministry of Commerce put 2006 dependency at 47 percent (up 4.1 points), and the row's own note says it stands around 50 percent; a Chinese Academy of Engineering researcher later…; and 14 more. 45 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The February 2007 ministry meeting record confirms seven cooperation instruments and separately describes RMB40 million humanitarian assistance. The amounts and instrument should be attributed to their sources. The signed loan terms and basis for the different debt totals remain unresolved. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The original citation is prepared House Foreign Affairs remarks delivered February 8. Attribute the two US-dollar figures to those remarks and keep the AidData protocol's two obligations at face value in their original currencies. The hearing’s two dollar figures are attributable to Lantos’s prepared statement. AidData’s cancellation record traces a separate protocol in RMB and links a second obligation. The palace facility and executed disbursement still require an instrument or government financial record. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The joint debt-sustainability report measures public and publicly guaranteed debt across creditors. It cannot reconcile a February 2007 announcement and the AidData protocol figures. Retain the source attribution and distinguish the stated palace funding offer from a signed interest-free infrastructure loan. Source recheck. China’s February 2007 foreign-ministry record documents the February 2 meeting, a separate RMB40 million humanitarian in-kind aid announcement for Darfur and the signing of seven economic and technical cooperation documents. paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CES-P4 — Part IV: China's Energy Security and U.S.–China Relations (O'Rourke; Blumenthal; Pollack, 2008/2012)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part IV (Chapters 18–20, Ebook pp. 429–476, 28 PDF pages, 103 endnotes) of *China's Energy Strategy: The Impact on Beijing's Maritime Policies* (Naval Institute Press, 2008 / 2012 Ebook ed.), `CES-P4` stages a direct strategic debate among Congressional Research Service naval specialist **Ronald O'Rourke** (Ch. 18), American Enterprise Institute fellow **Dan Blumenthal** (Ch. 19), and U.S. Naval War College professor **Jonathan D. Pollack** (Ch. 20) over whether China's global quest for energy and naval modernization portends inevitable Sino-U.S. conflict or an opportunity for managed maritime and energy interdependence.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 18 — China's Naval Modernization & Required U.S. Navy Capabilities (Ronald O'Rourke, PDF pp. 2–6, Table 1)**: Scores 14 USN investment areas across GWOT, Large-Scale Land, and China-Related scenarios (Table 1), warning that a GWOT-centered planning paradigm risks starving five high-end China programs (**a 2nd SSN/year, >1 CG(X)/year, sea-based terminal BMD replacement, Navy F-35C quantities, and ASW/AAW acquisitions**) and urging the new U.S. Maritime Strategy to elevate the China challenge without self-censorship.
• **Ch. 19 — Concerns with Respect to China's Energy Policy (Dan Blumenthal, PDF pp. 7–17, 58 notes)**: Critiques Beijing's mercantilist 'lock-up' energy diplomacy in **Sudan** (133,000 bpd, shielding Khartoum at the UNSC), **Iran** (287,000 bpd, $100B+ Sinopec/Zhuhai deals, SCO support), **Burma** (arms to SLORC, Indian Ocean port/intel access, 500-mile pipeline carrying only 200,000 bpd, and a diplomatic 'race to the bottom' with Tokyo and Delhi after the May 2003 Depayin massacre), and **Central Asia** (200,000 bpd Kazakhstan pipeline, 2005 SCO base-withdrawal statement, 21-gun salute for Uzbekistan's Karimov after Andijan, and 2 PLA armor-heavy mechanized corps), arguing China is undermining Robert Zoellick's 'responsible stakeholder' vision.
• **Ch. 20 — Energy Insecurity with Chinese and American Characteristics (Jonathan D. Pollack, PDF pp. 18–28, 45 notes)**: Directly rebuts Blumenthal's zero-sum framing, demonstrating that the U.S. (24.9% of world oil consumption) and China (8.2% of world oil consumption; a reported 94% domestic primary energy supply in 2005, with the estimate’s definition still unresolved) confront **'mutual assured dependence,'** that China's energy bureaucracy is fragmented and commercially competitive rather than a monolithic threat (quoting Lieberthal & Herberg and Miller), and that Washington should pursue a three-part agenda: bilateral Energy Policy Dialogue / IEA SPR integration, clean-coal/efficiency R&D, and maritime security cooperation under Adm. Mullen's **'1,000-ship Navy' (Global Maritime Partnership)** and USCG–CCG ties.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body: • **U.S. vs. China Energy & Trade Metrics**: Combined U.S. + China share of global oil consumption: `~35%` (`24.9%` U.S. on `2.5%` of world proven reserves vs. `8.2%` China on `1.4%` of world reserves, BP June 2006); Pollack reports 94% domestic primary energy self-sufficiency for China in 2005. The ratio of domestic production to consumption in the NBS June 2006 revision is 92.73%. The definition behind the 94% estimate remains open (CESP4-R29). Pollack’s U.S. import shares are >50% Western Hemisphere, <20% West/North Africa, and about 18% Middle East. The year, product scope and geographic groupings require confirmation (CESP4-R26, CESP4-R27) vs. China oil import sources: `25%` Africa, `17%` Saudi Arabia, `14%` Iran, `8%` Russia; **Sudan**: `133,000 bpd` to China (`#7` supplier, `2/3` of Sudan's exports; `$104M` debt write-off + `$17M` palace loan in Feb 2007); **Iran**: `287,000 bpd` in 2005 (`>15%` of PRC oil imports; bilateral trade `$2.49B` [2000] -> `$10.09B` [2005]); **Burma & Kazakhstan Pipelines**: `200,000 bpd` each (vs. China's `>200,000 bpd` annual oil import growth).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
The initial claim audits flagged a date slip in Ch. 19 Note 5. Zoellick’s statement was on December 8, 2005. Crucially, Blumenthal's correct statement on PDF p. 12 that China's oil import demand grows by *'more than 200,000 bpd each year'* provides a direct internal cross-check confirming the million-fold unit error (`'200,000 billion barrels'` per year) in Ch. 1 Note 33 (`[CESP1-R01]`).

**Energy institutions and import measures**: The State Council’s May 2005 decision created the National Energy Leading Group and placed its office within the National Development and Reform Commission. The group first met on June 2. A separate April precursor remains undocumented (CESP4-R36). For comparison with Pollack’s geographic shares, EIA reports 2.334 million barrels per day from its Persian Gulf grouping out of 13.714 million barrels per day in total U.S. crude oil and product imports in 2005, or 17.02%. Those figures apply to that year, product series and grouping. Pollack’s source definitions remain necessary for a direct comparison (CESP4-R26, CESP4-R27).

**Footnote rows**: all 102 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 81 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CESP4-S1N001 to CESP4-S2N044). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 102 notes: 26 (25%) are confirmed, 5 of them against a retrieved source and 21 after an outside web search (17 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 11 are flagged for reader check; 76 (75%) are not confirmed. Of the 76 notes not confirmed, 6 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 1 was judged not web-checkable (1 private interview or conversation); 69 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 81 source rows are 19 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 62 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CESP4-S1N012`: The sentence says over 80 percent of China's oil imports pass through the Strait of Malacca. Sources found give roughly 80 percent (a 2026 Foreign Policy piece), 77 percent, or 70 to 80 percent of energy imports; the share depends on the year and on whether crude only or all energy is counted; `CESP4-S1N019`: The sentence ranks Sudan as Beijing's seventh largest crude supplier at 133,000 barrels a day. Sources found give Sudan as fourth in 2002, about 97,000 b/d and eighth in 2006, and sixth in 2007, so rank and volume depend on the year; none matches seventh at 133,000; `CESP4-S1N023`: The sentence says Hu announced $104 million to write off Sudanese debt and $17 million for an interest-free loan or similar assistance (the sentence is cut off in the dataset); and 8 more. 11 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: 2002 port shutdown: forecast, daily rate and realized loss

rows.source: September 2008 oil-spill cooperation: exercise versus new agreement
rows.usage: The note is attached to: “It was announced in September 2008 that China was signing an agreement on mutual support for oil spill cleanup among Japan, Russia, South Korea, and China.”
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Correction established.** The official NOWPAP history dates adoption of its oil-spill contingency plan to 2003 and the regional cooperation memorandum to 2004. Its September 4, 2008 exercise report dates the Qingdao exercise to September 2. A newly recovered September 1 Xinhua report by Lin Hongmei, quoting the organizing maritime administration, also explicitly dates the four-country memorandum and mutual-assistance mechanism to November 2004. The report should distinguish the existing framework from the September 2008 exercise rather than imply that the mechanism was first being signed then. The exact September 3 newspaper item remains unrecovered.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The exact cited September 3 article and any distinct instrument it might have announced; this correction concerns chronology of the established framework.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** UNEP’s contemporary report identifies the September 2, 2008 Qingdao event as the second joint NOWPAP oil-spill exercise, organized by China and Korea with international observers. This corroborates practical cooperation but does not establish a new four-country agreement signed that September. Retrieve Lin Hongmei’s September 3 report and distinguish an exercise, an existing response framework and a new signing before changing the chronology. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The UNEP programme history gives three distinct milestones: the initial contingency plan in 2003, an exercise at Qingdao on September 2, 2008, and the 2008 amendment for hazardous substances. Align with CMS05-R07 and reserve judgment on what Lin's article announced until its text is found. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The contemporary UNEP exercise announcement and programme chronology support cooperation but give no evidence of a newly signed four-country instrument at the exercise. As in CMS05-R07, leave the precise press announcement open until Lin’s dated article is recovered. Source recheck. The transport ministry explicitly identifies the Qingdao event as a bilateral China–South Korea exercise under a regional framework. This corroborates the exercise and shows it cannot itself serve as proof of a new four-party signing. The dated publication by Lin Hongmei remains the missing source for the asserted announcement.

Coverage reconciliation. A shared search for Lin Hongmei’s September 3, 2008 dispatch did not recover the text. UNEP establishes the exercise and the earlier contingency framework, including a 2008 expansion. The cited announcement is still needed to determine what was described as a new agreement. The same lookup serves CMS05-R07.
evidence: PRC Ministry of Transport’s contemporaneous meeting account
Contemporary Lin Hongmei report quoting the exercise organizers

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CS21-P2 — Part II: Maritime Domain Awareness (Erickson; Smith; Goldstein; Moreland, 2010)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part II (Chapters 4–7, Ebook pp. 83–206, 76 PDF pages, 417 endnotes) of *China, the United States, and 21st-Century Sea Power: Defining a Maritime Security Partnership* (ed. Andrew S. Erickson, Lyle J. Goldstein, and Nan Li, Naval Institute Press, 2010), `CS21-P2` examines four operational arenas of nontraditional maritime security and Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA): container and port security (Erickson, Ch. 4), overseas and domestic counterterrorism (Smith, Ch. 5), Chinese coast guard institutional evolution (Goldstein, Ch. 6), and day-to-day U.S. Coast Guard–Chinese civil maritime engagement (Moreland, Ch. 7).

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 4 — The Container Security Initiative and U.S.–China Relations (Andrew S. Erickson, PDF pp. 2–30, 161 notes)**: Shows why Greater China (>42% of U.S.-bound cargo, 7 of the top 15 global container ports in Table 1) is central to supply-chain security; traces China's July 2003 accession to CSI (Hong Kong, Shanghai, Shenzhen) and related regimes (ISO 28000, ISPS, Megaports/SFI, EXBS, C-TPAT); highlights how China's **Nuctech (`威视股份`)** captured 90% of the domestic scanner market and exported to >60 countries; and explains why the U.S. H.R. 1 (2007) 100% scanning mandate proved technically and economically unfeasible and was postponed to 2014.
• **Ch. 5 — China's Power Ascendancy and the Global Terrorism Burden (Paul J. Smith, PDF pp. 31–46, 107 notes)**: Documents fatal terrorist/militant attacks on Chinese oil and construction workers in Sudan (Oct 2008), Pakistan (2004–2007), Ethiopia (Apr 2007), Nigeria, Niger, Afghanistan, and Kyrgyzstan (prompting CNPC to identify 18 'high-risk' countries), alongside Uighur unrest in Xinjiang (July 2009 Urumqi riot, Aug 2008 Kashgar/Kuqa attacks, and ETIM), comparing China's experience to the 20th-century U.S. 'great-power terrorism burden.'
• **Ch. 6 — Improving Chinese Maritime Enforcement Capabilities (Lyle J. Goldstein, PDF pp. 47–65, 119 notes)**: Draws on the 2007 Ningbo Maritime Police Academy study by **He Zhonglong et al. (`《中国海岸警卫队组建研究》`)** to profile China's fragmented **'five dragons stirring up the sea'** (~40,000 personnel across BCD Maritime Police, MSA, FLEC, GAC, and SOA/CMS) and their fleet disposition in Tables 1–2 (`8` large, `19` mid-size, `149` small cutters, `304` small boats).
• **Ch. 7 — U.S.–China Civil Maritime Operational Engagement (Capt. Bernard Moreland, USCG, PDF pp. 66–76, 30 notes)**: Details real-time 2006–2010 USCG–China operational cooperation in drug interdiction (*Jingyu 1*), North Pacific high-seas driftnet seizures (*Lu Rong Yu 6007*—10 Chinese driftnetters seized and 3 fined in 2007), ISPS/flag-state ship inspections, and AMVER–CHISREP open-ocean rescues (*Unicorn Ace*, *Hai Tong 7*, *Tong Cheng*, *Minpuyu*, *Fair Sky*).

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Container & Port Security Metrics (Ch. 4)**: Greater China share of U.S.-bound cargo: `>42%` (`11 of top 20` global container routes = `37.6%` of world volume); 2008 World Top 4 Ports (Table 1): `#1` Singapore (`29.9M` TEU), `#2` Shanghai (`28.0M`), `#3` Hong Kong (`24.5M`), `#4` Shenzhen (`21.4M`); Nuctech market share: `90%` of China domestic market (`147` airports) + `>220` scanner sets exported to `>60` countries.
• **'Five Dragons' Coast Guard Baseline (Ch. 6, Tables 1–2, 2007)**: Total personnel: `~40,000` (MSA `~20,000`, BCD Maritime Police `~10,000`, SOA/CMS `~6,000–8,000`, GAC `~2,000`, FLEC `~1,000`); Cutters by size: `8` Large (`3,500t+`), `19` Mid-size (`1,500t+`), `149` Small (`500t+`), `304` Boats (`100t+`); Aircraft: China `<36` (MSA ~11 helicopters, SOA 9 aircraft, BCD 0) vs. USCG `>200–250` and JCG `75`.

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
All 4 chapter-level reference rows (`CS21P2-R01` to `CS21P2-R04`) are rated `ok` (with 100% arithmetic verification across all four rows of Table 2 on p. 50). Comparing Goldstein's 2007/2010 Table 1 baseline (`8` cutters >3,500t and `19` cutters >1,500t across five fragmented agencies) with `CMGZ-00` (2019: unified PAP-subordinated CCG operating `>225` offshore ships >500t) provides one of the clearest quantitative measures of China's paranaval buildup in our corpus.

**Footnote rows**: all 413 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 328 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CS21P2-S3N001 to CS21P2-S8N030). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 413 notes: 119 (29%) are confirmed, 4 of them against a retrieved source and 115 after an outside web search (91 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is rated `fix`; 34 are flagged for reader check; 293 (71%) are not confirmed. Of the 293 notes not confirmed, 81 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 30 were judged not web-checkable (17 private interviews or conversations; 4 print-only books or paywalled items; 8 notes that are explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 1 other item); 182 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 328 source rows are 96 `ok`, 1 `fix` and 231 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CS21P2-S3N006`: The sentence says U.S. Customs invited China to join CSI in June 2002 and the process was completed the following year. The formal accession on 29 July 2003 is confirmed, but the sources found date China's agreement in principle to the 25 October 2002 Bush–Jiang meeting at Crawford and describe no earlier invitation from Customs; `CS21P2-S3N010`: The sentence says containers transport nearly 90 percent of global trade annually, a total of 153 million TEUs in 2008 (a 7 percent increase). The TEU total and growth match Drewry's estimate (152.8 million, up 7.2 percent); `CS21P2-S3N013`: The sentence says the average container ship emits 40 times less carbon dioxide than an aircraft. Studies found put air freight at roughly 44 times (a Defra comparison with a small container ship), 50 times, or up to 75 times (602 versus 8 g CO2 per ton-km) the emissions of shipping, depending on the vessel, aircraft and…; and 32 more. 94 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Taiwan democracy policy versus claims about presidential power and congressional consensus
rows.usage: Paraphrase of extracted passage, CS21P5-N076: Preserving Taiwan’s democracy is critically important, enjoys overwhelming congressional support, and cannot be changed by a U.S. president.
rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The original paragraph uses presidential-power language as part of an argument about durable political support for Taiwanese democracy. The Taiwan Relations Act establishes declared policy, not a measured consensus on every subsequent action or an unlimited legal prohibition on executive policy change. The cited State Department speech supports democracy while criticizing a specific referendum, further showing that policy support and particular decisions are distinct.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** A specified presidential action/authority and relevant congressional record; avoid converting the author’s political judgment into an absolute legal rule.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 11, 2026. The indexed State Department text identifies Christensen’s September 11, 2007 Annapolis speech A Strong and Moderate Taiwan and describes U.S. support for Taiwan’s democracy alongside moderation and strategic restraint. Direct access to the archive returned a technical-difficulties page, so the complete passage could not be read. The available policy language does not quantify congressional support or establish a legal limit on presidential power. Those stronger propositions require a contemporaneous voting or legislative record and clearer explanation of whether cannot is a political prediction or a legal claim. Consistency review, November 14, 2026. The AIT archive preserves the full Christensen speech. It affirms respect for Taiwan's democratic institutions and describes continuity across U.S. administrations. It supplies neither a quantified congressional consensus nor an independent legal rule restricting the president. Keep the policy attribution and those stronger claims separate. Follow-up review, November 14, 2026. The recovered AIT transcript speaks to continuity of policy and democratic practice. No vote or legal provision in that source establishes the quoted degree of congressional support or what future presidents are legally barred from changing. Source recheck. The statute states the relevant policy in 22 U.S.C. §3301, including a peaceful resolution and preservation of human rights. It neither measures congressional consensus about every action nor supplies a categorical bar on future executive policy change. Those statements require a specific roll call and discussion of particular presidential authority, rather than extrapolation from section 3301.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CS21-P5 — Part V: Future Prospects for U.S.–China Maritime Security Cooperation (Nan Li; Erickson; Yu Wanli; RAdm Yang Yi, 2010)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part V (Chapters 18–21, Ebook pp. 455–543, 55 PDF pages, 157 endnotes) of *China, the United States, and 21st-Century Sea Power* (Naval Institute Press, 2010), `CS21-P5` pairs U.S. Naval War College scholars **Nan Li** (Ch. 18) and **Andrew S. Erickson** (Ch. 19) with Peking University scholar **Yu Wanli** (Ch. 20) and PLA Navy **Rear Admiral Yang Yi** (Ch. 21) to evaluate whether the October 2007 U.S. *Cooperative Strategy for 21st Century Seapower* and the '1,000-ship Navy' / Global Maritime Partnership (GMP) can catalyze durable U.S.–China maritime cooperation despite structural distrust over Taiwan and U.S. naval primacy.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 18 — American and Chinese Naval Education (Nan Li, PDF pp. 2–11, 35 notes, Tables 1–4)**: Maps China's two-tier naval PME system (**Nanjing Naval Command College** and **Guangzhou Naval Arms Command College** in Table 1; **Dalian, Wuhan, Qingdao, Huludao, and Yantai** in Table 2), contrasts the U.S. liberal-arts -> specialization -> joint/coalition integration hourglass (Table 4) with China's specialized -> intraservice combined-arms pyramid (Table 3), and identifies **non-war military operations (MOOTW)** as a promising window for bilateral PME exchanges.
• **Ch. 19 — Chinese Views of America's New Maritime Strategy (Andrew S. Erickson, PDF pp. 12–37, 90 notes)**: Surveys Chinese media and three major assessments (**Lu Rude** in *People's Navy*, **Wang Baofu** in *Study Times*, and **Su Hao** in *Leaders*) of the 2007 U.S. Maritime Strategy; highlights how the U.S. document's misuse of **'multipolar'** fueled Chinese **'U.S. decline theory' (`衰落论`)**; and reviews bilateral cooperation (2006 SAREX, USCG ties, *Peace Ark* hospital ship) alongside proposals for a joint petroleum inventory system, SLOC threat database, and a U.S.–PRC incidents-at-sea code of conduct.
• **Ch. 20 — The American Factor in China's Maritime Strategy (Yu Wanli, PDF pp. 38–48, 31 notes)**: Traces PLAN strategy from coastal defense to near-seas defense, examines Mahan and Sun Yat-sen's influence, and contrasts Chinese 'sea power' proponents (**Zhang Wenmu**) with critics of the **'sea power trap'** (**Xu Qiyu, Tang Shiping, Ye Zicheng**).
• **Ch. 21 — A PLA Navy Perspective on Maritime Security Cooperation (RAdm Yang Yi, PDF pp. 49–55, 1 note)**: Urges China to move past a **'victim mentality'** and treat GMP as a **'thin wedge' / 'test-bed'** for incremental cooperation under four strict principles (UN authorization, sovereignty/non-intervention, non-traditional security focus, and no non-UN boardings/embargoes).

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **PLAN PME Institutions Mapped (Ch. 18, Tables 1–3)**: Advanced/Intermediate: **Nanjing Naval Command College** (Naval War College equivalent) & **Guangzhou Naval Arms Command College** (Surface Warfare School equivalent); Primary: **Dalian Naval Combatant Academy** (USNA equivalent; '4+1' dual-BA program), **Wuhan Naval Engineering University** (merged April 1999 with Nanjing Naval Electronics Engineering Academy; '4+1' & '2+2' NDSP tracks), **Qingdao Submarine Academy** (>40 foreign countries in maritime salvation class), **Huludao Naval Flight Academy**, and **Yantai Naval Aviation Engineering Academy**.
• **Strategic Concepts**: 'A Cooperative Strategy for 21st Century Seapower' (Oct 17, 2007) & 'Global Maritime Partnership / 1,000-Ship Navy'; 'Multipolarity' (`多极` / `一超多强`) vs. 'Multilateralism' & 'U.S. Decline Theory' (`衰落论`); 'Sea Power Trap' (`海权陷阱`, Xu Qiyu / Tang Shiping / Ye Zicheng); 'Shortest Stave of the Wooden Barrel' (Sino-U.S. military relations).

sections.heading: 4. Audit Assessment & Analytical Significance
sections.body:
All 4 reference rows (`CS21P5-R01` to `CS21P5-R04`) are rated `ok`. Within our dashboard, Nan Li's institutional mapping of the 7 PLAN academies in Ch. 18 (`[CS21P5-R01]`) provides the direct organizational key to the 38 doctoral and master's theses audited in Batch 1's **CMSI-87** (March 2013).

**Footnote rows**: all 156 footnotes were extracted and consolidated into 132 source rows in the Reference Audit Matrix (CS21P5-S2N001 to CS21P5-S4N031). Repeat citations of the same source within this paper, including Ibid. and short-form notes, share one row, which lists each note's passage and result. Footnote-level result: 156 notes: 35 (22%) are confirmed, 2 of them against a retrieved source and 33 after an outside web search (28 of the latter with a slip or an unchecked detail noted); 1 is flagged for reader check; 121 (78%) are not confirmed. Of the 121 notes not confirmed, 74 are Chinese-language sources that have not been searched in Chinese (a search in Chinese could settle some of them); 4 were judged not web-checkable (2 the authors' own data, imagery or analysis; 1 note that is explanatory text or a fragment, not a citation; 1 other item); 43 were searched on the web without finding corroboration. A source row is `ok` only when every note in it is confirmed, and `fix` when a note is confirmed wrong; the paper's 132 source rows are 28 `ok`, 0 `fix` and 104 `unk`. Notes flagged for reader check, for example (the outside search found something a reader should look at; none is a finding that the author is wrong): `CS21P5-N064`: The sentence says the then-commander of US forces in the Pacific, Adm. William Fallon, visited China in May and August 2006. Retrieved reports confirm the May 2006 trip (10 to 17 May) and, separately, a CMC vice chairman Guo Boxiong's July 2006 visit to the United States; no August 2006 Fallon visit was found. 42 notes carry a reader note on how the note is displayed or cited.

rows.source: Authorization for foreign state aircraft and the distress provision

rows.finding:
**Open-claim evidence follow-up, November 22, 2026 — Reviewed; unresolved.** The Chicago Convention puts state-aircraft authorization in Article 3 and assistance to aircraft in distress in Article 25. It does not expressly make the latter a waiver of the former. The supplied chapter qualifies the distress exception with perhaps, which should be preserved. Establishing a customary exception needs separate practice/commentary, not just juxtaposition of two treaty articles.

**Remaining gap or scope limit.** The cited Dugard passage and relevant state-aircraft practice supporting the proposed distress exception.

**Earlier audit record (preserved).** Reviewed November 13, 2026. Article 3(c) sets out authorization for state aircraft over or in another contracting state’s territory. Article 25 provides for practicable assistance to aircraft in distress. Because Article 3(a) distinguishes the Convention’s application to civil and state aircraft, Article 25 alone does not settle an exception for state aircraft. The cited Dugard article was not retrieved. Rechecked November 14, 2026. Article 3(d) adds the distinct undertaking to give due regard to the safety of civil navigation when issuing state-aircraft regulations. Article 25 concerns assistance by the territorial state. The provisions do not expressly create unilateral authorization for a state aircraft in distress. The suggested exception still needs an independent legal basis and the cited article. Follow-up review, November 15, 2026. The treaty places authorisation in its state-aircraft article and aircraft-in-distress assistance in a separate article. The text gives no express distress waiver of the authorisation provision. Establishing a customary exception would require the cited Dugard material or state practice on military aircraft.

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CAP-P2 — Part II: Chinese ISR and Counter-ISR (Mastalir; Dutton; Fisher; Hekler, 2011/2012)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Comprising Part II (Chapters 5–8, Ebook pp. 83–160, 49 PDF pages, 183 endnotes, and 2 technical appendices) of *Chinese Aerospace Power: Evolving Maritime Roles* (ed. Andrew S. Erickson and Lyle J. Goldstein, Naval Institute Press, 2011 / 2012 Ebook ed.), `CAP-P2` examines the four pillars of China's maritime intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), and counter-ISR architecture: space/counter-space assets (Mastalir, Ch. 5), legal control of maritime airspace and ADIZs (Dutton, Ch. 6), naval UAVs/UCAVs and spaceplanes (Fisher, Ch. 7), and airborne early warning (AEW&C) and electronic warfare (Hekler, Ch. 8).

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Ch. 5 — The PRC Challenge to U.S. Space Assets (Anthony J. Mastalir, PDF pp. 2–13, 42 notes)**: Analyzes China's Jan 2007 ASAT and Jan 2010 missile-intercept tests and 863 Program kinetic/directed-energy space weapons (Li Daguang 2001; Yuan Zelu 2005; >20 studies on 'new concept weapons' `新概念武器`), proposing an **International Security Space Alliance** and a **'thousand-sensor Shared Space Surveillance (SSS) architecture'** (Fig. 1) that includes China to deter covert orbital attacks.
• **Ch. 6 — China's Efforts to Assert Legal Control of Maritime Airspace (Peter A. Dutton, PDF pp. 14–24, 59 notes)**: Evaluates ADIZs and the April 2001 EP-3 collision under the Chicago Convention and UNCLOS, showing that only **23 of 163 coastal states** claim EEZ military restrictions and proving that ADIZ rules cannot legally restrict foreign military reconnaissance flights in international airspace above the EEZ (which covers 38% of world oceans).
• **Ch. 7 — Maritime Employment of PLA Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (Richard D. Fisher Jr., PDF pp. 25–36, 37 notes, Appendix of 17 UAV/UCAVs)**: Surveys China's UAV/UCAV surge at the 2006, 2008 (12 models), and Nov 2010 (>25 models) Zhuhai airshows and 2008/2010 CSAA 'Vanguard' conferences—profiling HALE/MALE UAVs (*Tianyi*, *Long Haul Eagle*, box-wing *Soar Dragon* [7,500 kg, 7,000 km], *Wing Loong*, *CH-3* with AR-1 missiles), jet UCAVs (*Dark Sword*, *Warrior Eagle*, Luoyang & NORINCO UCAVs with BA-7 missiles), VTUAVs (*LE 300*, *U8E*, saucer *D-1*), airships, and the Dec 2007 **Shenlong (`神龙`)** space plane.
• **Ch. 8 — Chinese Early-Warning Aircraft, Electronic Warfare, and Maritime C4ISR (Garth Hekler, PDF pp. 37–49, 45 notes, Appendix of 19 EW Systems)**: Audits **CNKI** literature (930 AEW&C, 1,049 EW aircraft, 6,805 EW, >200 DRFM papers), profiling the **KJ-2000**, **Shaanxi Y-8 'Gaoxin 1–7'** variants (including KJ-200/Gaoxin 5 AEW), CETC's **BM/KG300G airborne DRFM jammer pod**, Link-16-style **TIS** data links, bistatic TV/FM counter-stealth radars, and UAV jamming swarms.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Authored by U.S. Department of the Navy Senior Analyst Daniel J. Kostecka in *Chinese Aerospace Power: Evolving Maritime Roles* (Naval Institute Press, 2011 / 2012 Ebook ed., pp. 231–246), `CAP-C13` cuts through polarized Western speculation over China's aircraft carrier program (*Varyag* / *Liaoning*) by mining authoritative PLA doctrinal textbooks—the 2000 and 2006 editions of ***The Science of Campaigns* (`《战役学》`)**, the 2002 ***Campaign Theory Study Guide* (`《战役理论学习指南》`)**, and 1998 ***Winning High-Tech Local Wars***—alongside *Modern Navy* and *China Military Science*. Kostecka demonstrates that while STOBAR ski-jump constraints, rotary-wing AEW limitations, and India's 3-carrier force preclude U.S.-style sea dominance in the Indian Ocean, PLAN aircraft carriers and Type 071/LHD amphibious ships are tailor-made for regional East and South China Sea campaigns—specifically the **Coral Island Assault Campaign (`对珊瑚岛礁进攻战役`)** and **Sea Traffic Protection Campaign**—as well as far-seas **Non-Traditional Security (MOOTW)** missions.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **China's Aircraft Carrier & Air Wing Program (pp. 1–2)**: Documents the refurbishment of *Varyag* at Dalian (2005+), the **J-15 *Flying Shark*** fighter (first flight Aug 31, 2009; first ski-jump takeoff May 6, 2010), **9 Ka-31** and **Z-8 AEW** helicopters, and the **Y-7 fixed-wing AWACS** prototype pointing toward future CATOBAR carriers.
• **PLA Theory & Doctrinal Campaign Employment (pp. 2–5)**: Links Admiral Liu Huaqing's 1987 Pilot-to-Captain course at Guangzhou with the **Coral Island Assault Campaign** (2006 *Science of Campaigns*, stationing 1–2 carrier groups 100–150 nm offshore to cover distant reef landings in the South China Sea) and the **Sea Traffic Protection Campaign** (2002 *Campaign Theory Study Guide*, placing a carrier at the core of a mixed fleet with missile destroyers and SSNs), while explaining why STOBAR limits and Indian Navy land-based air/carrier superiority constrain wartime Indian Ocean carrier operations.
• **Vertical Assault & Non-Traditional Security Missions (pp. 6–8)**: Examines the **Type 071 LPD *Kunlunshan* (998)** and planned LHD vertical assault roles (citing *USS Eisenhower* off Haiti 1994 and *USS Kitty Hawk* in 2001), **HA/DR** lessons from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and 2008 Cyclone Nargis, and **NEO / peacekeeping protection** for **>5 million overseas Chinese** (45,000 in Nigeria, 24,000 in Sudan, 10,000 in Congo, 10,000 in Pakistan, plus ~1,000 PLA UN peacekeepers in Sudan/Congo).

paper_memo.memo_title: Analytical & Source-Audit Memo: CAP-C19 — Chinese Views of Sea-Based Ballistic Missile Defense (Toshi Yoshihara, 2011/2012)

sections.heading: 1. Strategic Context & Core Thesis
sections.body: Authored by U.S. Naval War College professor Dr. Toshi Yoshihara in *Chinese Aerospace Power: Evolving Maritime Roles* (Naval Institute Press, 2011 / 2012 Ebook ed., pp. 347–363), `CAP-C19` examines 40+ Chinese military and technical articles on U.S. and Japanese **Aegis sea-based Ballistic Missile Defense (BMD)** warships as a window into PLA counter-intervention strategy. Drawing on Wayne Hughes's (*Fleet Tactics*, 2000) insight that modern U.S. carrier strike groups concentrate their defensive firepower in a few Aegis cruisers and destroyers, Yoshihara shows that Chinese strategists view Aegis ships both as a strategic encirclement threat along China's periphery and as the decisive tactical center of gravity to be neutralized via a layered **Hierarchy of Anti-Aegis Tactics**—with **anti-ship ballistic missiles (ASBMs)** serving as Beijing's weapon of first resort to blind Aegis radars and exhaust VLS interceptor magazines.

sections.heading: 2. Section-by-Section Analytical Breakdown
sections.body:
• **Threat Assessment & 'Aegis Inundation' (pp. 1–2)**: Documents Chinese alarm over **'Aegis Ships Encircle China' (`宙斯盾舰合围中国`)** across three Pacific lines (**Yokosuka** as the boost-phase 'forward battlefield position' `前沿阵地`, **Pearl Harbor** for midcourse, **San Diego** for terminal, plus the Second/Third Island Chains as America's 'sea wall' `防波堤`) and the Feb 2008 Aegis satellite shoot-down.
• **The Japan Factor & Trilateral BMD Coalition (pp. 2–4)**: Tracks Chinese concern over JMSDF ***Kongō*- and *Atago*-class** SM-3 Block IIA upgrades, arguments that Aegis BMD blurs offense and defense by extending Japan's 'defense spearhead' (`防卫矛头`) and 'strategic space' (`战略空间`) to Taiwan, and warnings of a **'U.S.–Japan–Australia anti-ballistic missile coalition' (`美日澳反导联盟`)** along the First Island Chain.
• **Operational Assessments & China's Hierarchy of Anti-Aegis Tactics (pp. 4–8)**: Reviews Chinese ship-to-ship comparisons (*Ticonderoga* vs. *Kirov/Slava*; *Sovremenny* vs. *Kongō*) and air-saturation math (**150–200 Su-30s required to disable 8 Aegis ships** in *Naval & Merchant Ships*, Oct 2007), and reconstructs the PLA's three-tier anti-Aegis hierarchy: (1) high-risk ship-to-ship combat; (2) costly air-launched 'super saturation attacks' (`超饱和攻击`); and (3) **ASBMs armed with antiradiation and EMP submunitions** (citing p. 402 of the 2004 ***Science of Second Artillery Campaigns* [`《第二炮兵战役学》`]**) to inflict **'mission kills'** on Aegis radars and **exhaust SM-3/SM-6 VLS magazines** ahead of follow-on air and submarine cruise-missile strikes.

sections.heading: 3. Key Doctrinal Concepts, Terminology & Quantitative Claims
sections.body:
• **Chinese Anti-Aegis & BMD Terms**: 'Aegis Ships Encircle China' (`宙斯盾舰合围中国`) & 'Aegis Inundation' (`宙斯盾泛滥`); 'Anti-Ballistic Missile Net' (`导弹防御网`); 'Forward Battlefield Position' (`前沿阵地`, Yokosuka) & 'Sea Wall' (`防波堤`, 2nd/3rd Island Chains); 'U.S.–Japan–Australia Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition' (`美日澳反导联盟`); 'Super Saturation Attacks' (`超饱和攻击`).
